_about: Labelled answers for the AI-assisted-answer detector. Four tiers. 'ai_*' texts were written by an LLM (Claude, 2026-11-06) to the same RN questions; 'human_*' texts are synthetic phone-speech transcripts written to sound like real candidates. Nothing here is a real candidate. Add redacted real-call transcripts to fixtures/real/ and they are picked up automatically.

questions.q_judgment: Tell me about a time a patient started going downhill on your shift. What did you notice, and what did you do?
questions.q_communication: Tell me about a time a patient or family member was upset. What did you say or do?
questions.q_teamwork: Tell me about a shift where you were short-staffed. How did you get through it?
questions.q_meds: Walk me through how you handle a medication you have never given before.

answers.text: During a night shift, I noticed that a post-operative patient's heart rate had gradually increased while his blood pressure trended downward. Additionally, he appeared more confused than he had been at the start of my shift. I immediately performed a focused assessment, rechecked his vital signs, and notified the charge nurse. I then escalated to the rapid response team and communicated my findings using the SBAR format. Ultimately, the patient was transferred to a higher level of care, and I believe my early recognition contributed to a positive outcome.
answers.follow_up_text: I believe it was approximately two hours into the shift. I ensured that all documentation was completed appropriately.

answers.text: I recall a situation where a family member was upset because they felt their loved one's pain was not being managed effectively. First, I listened actively and acknowledged their concerns without becoming defensive. Second, I explained the current pain management plan in clear, simple terms and checked their understanding. Finally, I collaborated with the provider to reassess the plan and communicated the updates to the family promptly. It is important to maintain empathy and professionalism in these situations, and I always make sure the family feels heard.
answers.follow_up_text: I communicated the updated plan to them as soon as the provider approved it, which helped to rebuild trust.

answers.text: On a shift where we were significantly short-staffed, I prioritized patient safety by reassessing acuity levels and reorganizing my workflow accordingly. I communicated proactively with the charge nurse to ensure that critical tasks were covered and delegated appropriate tasks to our nursing assistant. Furthermore, I maintained open communication with my colleagues so that we could support one another throughout the shift. Overall, the experience reinforced the importance of teamwork, flexibility, and clear communication in delivering safe and effective patient care.
answers.follow_up_text: The nursing assistant handled vital signs and ambulation so that I could focus on medication administration.

answers.text: When I encounter a medication I have not administered before, I follow a structured approach to ensure patient safety. First, I review the medication in a reputable drug reference to understand its indications, dosage, contraindications, and potential adverse effects. Second, I verify the order against the patient's allergies, weight, and renal function as appropriate. Third, I consult with the pharmacist or a senior colleague if I have any uncertainty. Finally, I educate the patient about the medication and monitor them closely after administration.
answers.follow_up_text: I would typically utilize the hospital's approved drug reference and consult pharmacy when appropriate.

answers.text: I once cared for a patient with pneumonia whose oxygen saturation began to decline despite supplemental oxygen. I noticed increased work of breathing and a subtle change in mental status. I promptly increased the oxygen as permitted by protocol, repositioned the patient, and obtained a full set of vital signs. I then notified the provider and the rapid response team and prepared the patient for possible transfer. Throughout the process, I remained calm and communicated clearly with the patient and the team, which I believe is essential in these situations.
answers.follow_up_text: I documented the interventions and the patient's response in a timely and comprehensive manner.

answers.text: A patient was frustrated because she had been waiting for her discharge paperwork for several hours. I approached her calmly, apologized for the delay, and explained the steps that remained in the discharge process. Additionally, I provided her with a realistic timeframe and checked back regularly to keep her informed. I also advocated on her behalf by following up with the provider and case management. By the time she left, she expressed her appreciation for the clear communication. I believe transparency and follow-through are key to maintaining patient trust.
answers.follow_up_text: I followed up with case management twice to ensure the paperwork was prioritized appropriately.

answers.text: So there was a post-op patient, um, his heart rate was creeping up and his pressure was drifting down over a couple hours, and he seemed a bit more confused than earlier. I did a quick focused assessment, rechecked everything, and let the charge nurse know. Then I called rapid response and gave them an SBAR. He ended up going to step-down. I think catching it early made a real difference for him.
answers.follow_up_text: Um, I'd say about two hours in. I made sure the charting was all done after.

answers.text: There was a daughter who was really upset because she felt like her mom's pain wasn't being managed well. So I just listened first, let her say everything, and didn't get defensive about it. Then I explained the pain plan in plain language and made sure she understood it. And I went to the provider to get the plan reassessed and came back and told her what changed. I think the main thing is just making sure the family actually feels heard.
answers.follow_up_text: I told her as soon as the provider signed off on the new orders, which helped a lot with trust.

answers.text: We were really short one night so, uh, I basically re-sorted my patients by who was sickest and reorganized how I was going to move through the shift. I kept the charge nurse in the loop so the critical stuff was covered, and I handed off vitals and walking patients to our aide. And we all just kept talking to each other all night so nobody got buried. Honestly it reminded me how much it comes down to communication and being flexible.
answers.follow_up_text: The aide took vitals and ambulation so I could stay on top of meds.

answers.text: If it's a med I've never given, I've got kind of a routine. I look it up first, what it's for, the dose, what to watch for. Then I check it against the patient's allergies and their weight and kidney function if that matters for it. If I'm not sure about anything I'll ask pharmacy or one of the more experienced nurses. And then I explain it to the patient and keep a closer eye on them after I give it.
answers.follow_up_text: Usually Lexicomp, uh, the hospital's reference, and I'll call pharmacy if I'm unsure.

answers.text: I had a pneumonia patient whose sats kept dropping even on oxygen. I noticed he was working harder to breathe and was just a little off mentally. So I bumped the oxygen up per protocol, sat him up, got a full set of vitals, and then called the provider and rapid response and got him ready in case he needed to move. I just tried to stay calm and keep everyone, including him, in the loop the whole time.
answers.follow_up_text: I charted everything I did and how he responded right after.

answers.text: A patient was pretty frustrated because her discharge paperwork had been sitting for hours. I went in, apologized for the wait, and walked her through what was actually left in the process. I gave her a realistic time and kept checking back so she wasn't in the dark. I also kept pushing the provider and case management for her. By the time she left she actually thanked me. I think being transparent and following through is what keeps people's trust.
answers.follow_up_text: I went back to case management twice to make sure her paperwork was moving.

answers.text: Um okay so, there was this one guy, he was a post-op, um, hip, and like around two in the morning his heart rate was, it was like one ten and it had been in the eighties. And he was, he kept asking me where he was, which, he wasn't like that at the start. So I I rechecked everything, his pressure was ninety over fifty something, and I grabbed my charge nurse, I was like, I don't like this. We called rapid and I mean they came up and he ended up going to step-down. It was, yeah, it was scary but we caught it.
answers.follow_up_text: Um, it was, I want to say two, maybe two thirty? Yeah. I remember because I had just finished my other guy's two a.m. meds.

answers.text: Oh gosh, um, so there was a daughter, her mom was in a lot of pain and she was, she was yelling at me basically in the hallway. And honestly my first instinct was to like defend myself but I didn't, I just, I let her go, I let her finish. And then I said look, I hear you, let me go check what's ordered. And the PRN was due anyway so I gave it, and I went and paged the doc about bumping it up. And I came back and told her what I did. She was, she calmed down a lot after that, she actually apologized later.
answers.follow_up_text: Uh, I said something like, I'm sorry, you're right, she's hurting, let me fix this. Something like that.

answers.text: Ugh, yeah, we had a night where two people called out so it was like, I had seven patients instead of five. Um, so I just, I kind of went room to room first thing and figured out who was gonna be a problem, you know, who was sick sick. And our aide, Marcus, he was amazing, he did all my vitals and like got people to the bathroom. And me and the other nurse we just kept yelling across the hall like, you good? I'm good. Um, we got through it. Nobody fell. That was my goal.
answers.follow_up_text: He did vitals and, um, he helped me turn my big guy in twelve, the one who was like three hundred pounds.

answers.text: Um, okay so if I've never given it, I'm, honestly I'm looking it up on Lexicomp on the computer first, like what is this, what's it for. And then I'll, I'll ask whoever's around, like hey have you given this, what do you watch for. And if it's something weird like a drip I've never hung I'll call pharmacy, they don't mind. Um, and then I tell the patient, hey this is new for you, this is what it does, let me know if you feel funny. And I just check on them more.
answers.follow_up_text: Lexicomp, yeah, and I mean pharmacy. Pharmacy's always been good to me.

answers.text: So I had a lady with pneumonia and she was on like four liters and she was satting fine, ninety four, and then she just, she started dropping, like ninety, eighty eight. And she was, you could see her shoulders going, like she was working. And she got kind of, kind of sleepy, which, she had been chatty. So I went up on the oxygen, I sat her up, I I called the doc and honestly I called rapid at the same time because I didn't want to wait. They put her on BiPAP and she went to the unit.
answers.follow_up_text: Um, she went to BiPAP, yeah, and then the ICU took her like an hour later I think.

answers.text: There was a lady who'd been waiting on her discharge papers since like noon and it was four and she was, she was done, she was packing her bag. And I just went in and I was like, I'm so sorry, this is ridiculous, let me find out what's going on. And it turned out the doc hadn't signed the med rec. So I, I tracked him down, I literally walked to the physician's lounge. Um, and I came back and told her, it's signed, give me twenty minutes. And she was okay after that. She just wanted someone to actually do something.
answers.follow_up_text: I I told her like, okay it's signed, I just need to print your meds and go over them, twenty minutes.

answers.text: Sure. The one I always think about is a post-op hip patient on a night shift a couple of years ago. Around two a.m. his heart rate climbed from the eighties to about one ten and his pressure dropped to ninety over fifty, and he started asking where he was. I rechecked his vitals, told my charge nurse, and we called a rapid response. I gave SBAR to the team when they arrived. He went to step-down and turned out to be bleeding internally. What I took from it was to trust the trend, not the single number.
answers.follow_up_text: About two, two thirty. I remember because I had just finished my two a.m. med pass on the other side of the hall.

answers.text: A daughter was upset in the hallway because her mother was in pain and felt ignored. I let her finish, told her she was right that her mom was hurting, and said I would go check the orders. The PRN was due so I gave it, then paged the physician about increasing the dose, and I went back and told her exactly what I had done and when to expect relief. She calmed down, and later in the shift she apologized to me. The lesson for me was to lead with the action, not the explanation.
answers.follow_up_text: I said something like, you're right, she's hurting, let me fix this. Then I went and did it.

answers.text: We had a night where two nurses called out and I went from five patients to seven. I rounded on everyone first to figure out who was the sickest, and I asked our aide Marcus to take vitals and bathroom trips so I could stay on meds and assessments. The other nurse and I checked in with each other every hour. Nobody fell and every med was on time, which was my goal for the night. Afterward I asked the manager about a float pool, which they did eventually add.
answers.follow_up_text: Marcus did vitals and helped me turn a three hundred pound patient in room twelve.

answers.text: If I have never given a medication, I look it up in Lexicomp first, so I know the indication, the dose range, and what to monitor. Then I check the order against the patient's allergies, weight, and labs. If anything is unclear I call pharmacy, and if it is a drip I have never hung I ask a senior nurse to double check the pump with me. Then I tell the patient it is new for them, what it does, and what to report. I check on them more often for the first hour.
answers.follow_up_text: Lexicomp, and pharmacy. For a drip, I ask a senior nurse to verify the pump settings with me.

answers.text: I had a pneumonia patient on four liters who had been satting ninety four and started dropping to the high eighties. She was using her shoulders to breathe and had gone from chatty to sleepy. I increased her oxygen per protocol, sat her upright, and called both the physician and the rapid response team because I did not want to wait. She went on BiPAP and was moved to the ICU about an hour later. The change in her mental status was the thing that told me not to wait.
answers.follow_up_text: BiPAP first, on the floor, and then the ICU took her about an hour after that.

answers.text: A patient had been waiting since noon for discharge paperwork and by four she was packing her bag. I apologized, found out the physician had not signed the medication reconciliation, and walked to the physician lounge to get it signed. I came back and told her it was done and she would be out in twenty minutes, and she was. People mostly want to see someone actually do something, so I try to come back with an action rather than an update.
answers.follow_up_text: I told her it was signed and I needed twenty minutes to print and review her medications.
